I Want My MTV
EYE WONT my EM-tee-vee
interjection, phrase (Gen X slang)
The slogan of MTV’s 1982 advertising campaign, created by adman George Lois, in which rock stars such as Mick Jagger, Pete Townshend, and Pat Benatar looked into the camera and told viewers to call their local cable company and demand the young channel: "I want my MTV!" The campaign worked, and the line became a catchphrase. Sting sang it as the opening hook of Dire Straits’ "Money for Nothing" (1985), a song that mocked rock stardom and its easy money, and whose computer-animated video became an MTV staple.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

I want my MTV was an advertising slogan that became a generation’s chant: a demand, shouted by famous rock stars, that the cable company hand over the new music channel. The campaign was brilliant because it put the words of entitlement in the viewer’s own mouth. I want. My. The Christian observation is that the most famous psalm in the Bible begins with the opposite sentence: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psa 23:1). The slogan teaches a child to want; the psalm teaches him to rest. Advertising works by multiplying wants, and the Ten Commandments end by naming that very sin: "Thou shalt not covet" (Exo 20:17). Paul learned the counter-skill in prison: "Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Php 4:11). "Godliness with contentment is great gain" (1Ti 6:6). James explains where unchecked wanting leads — "Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain… ye have not, because ye ask not" (Jas 4:2) — and Hebrews gives the reason contentment is possible at all: "be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee" (Heb 13:5). The slogan was right about one thing: what we want, we will demand. A father can teach his children to recognize the voice of the advertiser in their own mouths, and to answer it with the shepherd’s psalm. We have a Shepherd; we shall not want.

Webster 1828 Definition

MTV’s 1982 ad slogan (George Lois; later the hook of Dire Straits’ "Money for Nothing," 1985) that put a consumer’s demand in a generation’s mouth; Scripture answers, The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want (Psa 23:1).

I WANT MY MTV, interj. (Gen X slang, 1982–mid-1980s, US advertising) Slogan of MTV’s campaign urging viewers to demand the channel from their cable company; later a catchphrase for any insistent demand. "No cable? I want my MTV!"

Spoken in the ads by stars including Mick Jagger, Pete Townshend, and Pat Benatar; created by adman George Lois.

Sung by Sting as the opening hook of Dire Straits’ "Money for Nothing" (1985).

Webster 1828: WANT, n. 1. Deficiency; defect; the absence of that which is necessary or useful; as a want of power or knowledge for any purpose; want of food and clothing. …

Decode for parents: the slogan trains wanting; the psalm trains resting. Teach your children to hear the difference.

Key Scripture

Psa 23:1 — "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want."

Php 4:11 — "Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content."

1Ti 6:6 — "But godliness with contentment is great gain."

Jas 4:2 — "Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not."

Heb 13:5 — "Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee."

Modern Corruption

I want my MTV put the advertiser’s demand in the consumer’s mouth and taught a generation to want out loud; Scripture answers with the shepherd’s contentment: I shall not want.

expand to see more

Manufactured wanting. The genius of the campaign was that it did not ask anyone to like MTV; it told them they already wanted it and should be angry not to have it. That is the engine of modern advertising, and a child raised in front of it learns to feel deprived of things he had never heard of a week before. James traces where restless desire leads: to quarrels and covetousness (Jas 4:2). The tenth commandment is not old-fashioned; it is the one our economy most depends on our breaking.

The shepherd’s answer. Psalm 23 begins where the slogan ends: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want (Psa 23:1). Paul calls contentment something he "learned" (Php 4:11), which means it can be taught at home. Godliness with contentment is great gain (1Ti 6:6), and it rests on a promise better than any channel: I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee (Heb 13:5). A child who learns that sentence by heart will hear the advertiser’s voice for what it is, and will not need to obey it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old Norse vanta (to lack) → English want → MTV’s 1982 campaign → Dire Straits’ "Money for Nothing" (1985) → catchphrase of demand; Scripture: I shall not want (Psa 23:1).

expand to see more

Old Norse vanta — to lack, be missing; English want — lack, then desire

1981 MTV launches; many cable systems decline to carry it

1982 George Lois campaign: rock stars say "I want my MTV!" and viewers call their cable companies

1985 Sting sings the hook on Dire Straits’ "Money for Nothing"

Biblical want: the shepherd’s sheep shall not want (Psa 23:1); content in every state (Php 4:11)

"The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want (Psa 23:1)."
